name: K.S. Bhullar, R&AW Special Secretary
role: RAW Special Secretary — institutional skeptic and bureaucratic counterweight to Sanyal
real_life_inspiration: A.S. Dulat — former RAW Chief (1999–2000) and long-time Intelligence Bureau operative. Dulat was RAW chief during the IC-814 period and is known for his nuanced, dialogue-first approach to Kashmir and Pakistan — diametrically opposed to Doval's doctrine. Wrote critically about the hawkish turn in Indian intelligence in his memoir 'The Spy Chronicles' (co-authored with Pakistani ISI general Asad Durrani).

inspiration_notes.as_dulat_parallel: A.S. Dulat served as RAW chief 1999-2000 — precisely the IC-814 era. His pragmatic, engagement-oriented approach to Pakistan intelligence contrasts sharply with Doval's offensive posture. The film uses this ideological friction to dramatise the institutional debate.
inspiration_notes.spy_chronicles: Dulat's book 'The Spy Chronicles' (2018), co-authored with Pakistani ISI general Asad Durrani, was controversial in India for suggesting dialogue with Pakistan. The book was seen as going against the grain of the post-2016 hawkish consensus — exactly what Bhullar represents in the film.
inspiration_notes.ib_vs_raw_dispute: IB is technically domestic intelligence; RAW handles external. Sanyal as IB Director running Pakistan operations is the institutional boundary violation that Bhullar (as RAW's representative) disputes. This turf war is well-documented in Indian intelligence literature.
inspiration_notes.film_arc: In Film 1, Bhullar is the voice arguing for 'strategic patience' and opposing Operation Dhurandhar. His arc tracks the UPA-era institutional consensus. In Film 2 (Naya Bharat era), he is sidelined — Sanyal's approach has been politically vindicated.
